subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON SALE OF TRANSPORT PLANES TO UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON SALE OF TRANSPORT PLANES TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last, in reply to a question asked by the
Leader of the Opposition, I confirmed that negotiations were in progress for the sale of transport planes by a Canadian company to two United States companies. Canadair Limited have today announced the successful conclusion of negotiations and have made sales of 5 CL-44 turboprop cargo aircraft to Seaboard and Western Airlines Inc., and 10 of the same planes to the Flying Tiger Line, Inc. These two lines are reported to be the largest air cargo carriers in the world.
A few weeks ago Canadair Limited approached the Export Credits Insurance Corporation asking for insurance in connection with the proposed sale of these 15 aircraft. The amount involved is approximately $70 million. The terms of payment are 10 per cent cash with order, a further 10 per cent on delivery, and the balance of 80 per cent spread in instalments over five years after delivery. The policies will protect Canadair Limited against non-payment by the buyers for up to 85 per cent of the amount owing.
It should be noted that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation does not finance. It insures against non-payment. In the normal course of events the exporter arranges for any necessary financing with his own bankers, and I understand that such arrangements have been made by Canadair through Canadian banking channels. These two orders for 15 aircraft will provide employment over a period of two and one half years for 4,500 men, many of whom are professionals or in the skilled category.

Mr. Speaker, investment transactions are the investments constituting the use of moneys standing to the credit of the fund for the purpose of acquiring obligations. If you look at the marginal note opposite section 85 (1), there you will see the word "investments". When you come to section 86 it is "advances" which are talked about. You are in a different realm there. Section 20 and section 85 relate to investment in these government obligations. When you come to section 86 you are dealing with amounts. You are not dealing with investment there at all, but with amounts in the fund. Then when the amounts are not adequate, provision is made for a loan.
Now, a loan is not an investment transaction within the contemplation of section 20 at all. It is not an investment. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, so far as any suggestion of investment is concerned, under section 86 it is an investment on the part of the Minister of Finance, and the statute deals very precisely with the terms upon which the Minister of Finance may make a loan for the benefit of the fund to enable it to meet its obligations.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so far as the purchase and sale of securities not related under section 86 to loans are concerned, that of course is done by the investment committee appointed in accordance with the terms of section 20, and that has been done with strict adherence to the terms of the act. But when you come to section 86, this is not a matter of investment by the fund or the commissioners. This is a matter of borrowing by the fund and by the commissioners. The investment here is on the part of the Minister of Finance in the form of a loan, and the statute has dealt with this in the plainest terms. The statute says that the Minister of Finance may in the given circumstances make this loan on the terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, and that was done.

Unemployment Insurance Act hand and three or four of the hon. gentlemen along this side on the other, I think if Cervantes were still alive and preparing his book "Don Quixote" he could very well have had all four of them in his book as characters.
The Minister of Finance, if nothing else, I think, has certainly given some truth to the old saying that figures do not lie but liars ofttimes figure.
It is unfortunate, I think, that in considering this particular bill which is before us, which relates to unemployment insurance, unemployment insurance payments, benefits and so on, the whole discussion should be cluttered up, as I think it has been, with references to hidden or secret reports and references to charges of lawbreaking on the part of the Minister of Labour. All these points about the budget, secret documents, hiding reports, breaking the law and so on have absolutely nothing to do with the bill itself. I think that is what we should be addressing ourselves to; we should be looking at the bill in the light of exactly what it is and why such a bill needs to be introduced at this time. I certainly think the reckless use of the unemployment insurance fund by the minister without any consideration for safeguards and proper methods of replenishing the fund is the reason we are in this position today. I would like to put a few short statements on record to indicate the position of the C.C.F. party with regard to this particular bill.
The bill, in effect, asks the working class people of this country to subsidize the unemployment policy of the government; it imposes an additional tax burden on workers without any comparable benefits accruing to them. It is certainly an indication of the government's lack of intestinal fortitude-or to use plain terms, guts-to replenish the fund in a sensible way from general revenue, and to declare this heavy drain on the fund as part of a national disaster rather than asking the working classes themselves to bail the government out of its difficult position.
I am sure the minister does not seriously expect members of this group, particularly, to support this bill. We have no intention of supporting it, because we regard it as a back door, sneaky method of imposing taxation on second reading of this bill. If the minister wishes to withdraw the bill and introduce something which is more in keeping with ethics and more in keeping with


a sound moral attitude toward the working class we would be prepared to look at it again, but we are certainly not prepared to accept the measure as it stands in the light of the principles which it contains.

speechtext:
should like to make one or two comments on this bill at this time, and I should prefer to stick closely to the principles of the bill rather than raise a verbal smoke screen of the type we have had from the Minister of Finance this afternoon.
There are some things in this bill with which I agree. That clause which refers to the increase in the wage ceiling is one which I think has a great deal of merit. Over the years the workers of this country have enjoyed the benefit of increased wages, and it is understandable that some of them should have exceeded the limits which were imposed in the original act. I think raising this ceiling from $4,800 to $5,460 is a good thing to do, because it will bring into the insurance scheme, according to the statement made by the minister, another 80,000 wage earners who will become eligible for the benefits of the unemployment insurance plan.
I think, too, that the proposed increase in the benefit period from 36 to 52 weeks has some merit. If a worker can qualify under the terms of the regulations for benefits throughout a period of 52 weeks, I see nothing wrong with that. I can understand that a situation may arise in which a worker may be unemployed for this length of time. I hope that such would not be the case, and I certainly hope there will never be a large number of people in Canada who will require unemployment insurance for 52 weeks; but for the small number who do need it, and who are able to qualify, I think this will be of great assistance, and I certainly have no objection to this proposed amendment.
Again, I have no objection to the revision of the allowable earnings. I agree with the minister in his division of allowable earnings into two classes-those paid to workers with dependents, and those paid to workers without dependents. I should think, however, some thought might be given to consolidating the two or three lower classes. After all, it is understandable that a man who receives $6 in unemployment insurance for a week will need $4, $5 or $6 just as badly as a person who receives $12 or $15; and if during the winter time a worker gets $6 or $8 a week and is able to obtain a day or two shovelling snow, I see no reason why the amount of benefit he is able to obtain should be limited by the fact that he receives a lower rate than another man who lives nearby. However, I have no objection to this amendment.

The main purpose of the bill, however, is to stabilize the unemployment insurance fund. Over the last two years this fund has been considerably depleted. It has been depleted by an amount estimated to be $400 million. I agree that this money has been paid out to those who were suffering from the effects of unemployment, and that it has helped to relieve a large measure of the distress felt by those who have had the misfortune to be unemployed. These benefits went out not only to those who were seasonally unemployed but also to a large number who were qualified for regular unemployment insurance benefits.
But if the main purpose of this bill is to stabilize the fund, let us look at the manner in which this is being done. First of all, the contributions made by wage earners are being increased by anywhere between 25 per cent and 30 per cent. In return for this larger contribution they are receiving no extra benefits, nothing more than they have received in the past. Again, employers will be obliged to increase their contributions by between 25 and 30 per cent.
We are living in a country where prices are high, and any charge which is going to increase the cost of living, or any charge which will have the effect of increasing the cost of production and particularly the cost of articles which we sell in foreign markets, will only result in our being placed in a less competitive position. This amendment will certainly increase our cost of production at a time when corporation taxes in this country are at the highest level in our history. I feel sure that this bill will give little encouragement to those who wish to improve or extend their industrial interests.
For example, I have here a clipping taken from this morning's Montreal Gazette. The headline says "Industry Asks Tax Be Eased" and the first paragraph reads as follows:
The federal government was urged today to grant substantial tax concessions to Canada's forest industries to enable them to remain competitive in world markets, particularly in the field of pulp and paper.
And the last paragraph reads as follows:
Canada has become less and less attractive for major investment in this field. Investment is flowing elsewhere. There is obviously something seriously wrong with the economic climate for the pulp and paper industry in Canada.
Yet despite this, in addition to the high level of taxes which industry already has to pay, the minister is imposing this extra charge by way of the employer's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. Speaking the other day on the resolution I said this was nothing more than an extra tax of something over $70 million which will be imposed on the workers and employers in this
Unemployment Insurance Act country. I still think that is so, because no extra benefit is being received from it.
As far as the administration of the fund is concerned, there can be no doubt that a great deal of information is needed regarding the handling of the fund in the last two years. The Minister of Finance may quibble all he likes about the $10 million that was lost due to the cashing of some of the bonds held by the unemployment insurance commission, but the money is lost, nevertheless. One might ask, are the workers of this country now being required to make up this $10 million? Is that what the government is doing?
We could ask a number of other questions about the investments of the commission. The minister says the commission is quite within its rights in cashing any of its investments at any time it wishes to do so. If that be so, why was it necessary to borrow the sum of $55 million from the government? I do not know the reason; but one might ask the government, if the question does not embarrass them, to what extent it was due to the bond conversion operation and its effects upon the bond market.
After all, as unemployment increases there comes a critical point beyond which benefits paid to our people begin to move from the realm of insurance into the realm of welfare. Because of the large amount of unemployment we have had in the last two years it is my belief that the government should have made up this deficit in the unemployment insurance fund by a direct grant. What we are now doing is asking a certain proportion of the workers of this country to pay for that which more properly should have been considered as a welfare payment. I might say, to quote Kipling, that we are "robbing a selected Peter to pay a collective Paul".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to make a few brief remarks on the second reading of Bill No. C-43, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. To my way of thinking, this bill is nothing else but another measure introduced by the present government which takes away so much from the taxpayers but offers so little in return.
We listened for a while before the adjournment yesterday afternoon and again for over half an hour this afternoon to the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). We learned at last in the course of his remarks that the minister himself is admitting the present weakness of the bond market. We also received from the minister certain information which up to now had been kept away from the members of this house. For obvious reasons, reasons known to any hon.

Unemployment Insurance Act member who was in the house in the spring of 1956, the present Minister of Finance should be the last member to accuse members of this house of not abiding by the rules of the house. We certainly have not forgotten his attitude on that occasion.
In introducing the resolution preceding this bill, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) clearly stated that the purpose of the amendment was to give stability to the unemployment insurance fund. The unemployment insurance fund was built up of contributions from employees and employers, together with certain contributions from the federal treasury, and during the regime of the former administration had exceeded the sum of $900 million. The fact remains that after fewer than two years of administration by the present government the workers' fund has been reduced to a sum under $500 million.
We have been asked to approve the second reading of a measure which has been introduced by the present administration to cover up its failure to provide sound and consistent policies in the administration of the affairs of this country. This is a clear illustration of the greater concern of the present government in trying to keep some of its election promises than in giving the country sound management. In moving the second reading of this bill the minister stated, as reported at page 3537 of Hansard:
The present amendments in this bill will provide coverage for a greater number of wage earners.
No one on this side of the house has any objection to the fact that a greater number of wage earners will be included under unemployment insurance benefits; but the main class of wage earners who are now being included are the class of wage earners who are earning salaries ranging from $5,000 to $6,000 a year, and they are the ones who are in less need of unemployment insurance benefits.
Further on, the minister stated that these amendments will increase benefits and allowable earnings. They certainly will not increase the rate of benefits which are being given now under the present regulations. In order to get increased benefits the wage earners will have to earn larger salaries and they will have to make larger contributions.
The minister also stated that these amendments will also increase contributions. There is no doubt in anyone's mind that one of the main amendments of this bill is designed to increase contributions. This is why I say the measure introduced by the present administration is another one which will take away so much but it will offer so little in return. In fact, it will ask the wage earners

of this country and the employers of this country to pay 30 per cent more in their contributions to the unemployment insurance fund.
The amendments also propose to increase the benefit period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks. At the resolution stage preceding the bill the Minister of Labour stated that this is one of the promises made by this government during the last two campaigns. The minister appeared to be proud to be able to advise the house and the country that they were increasing the unemployment insurance benefit period of 36 weeks to 52 weeks; but the minister did not state that when they promised the electors of this country to extend the benefit period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks that at the same time they would ask them to contribute 30 per cent more to the unemployment insurance fund by way of premiums.
These additional premiums, Mr. Speaker, are an additional tax added to the taxpayers of this country. As was stated the other day by my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten), it is an additional tax of $72 million over and above the increased taxation of $352 million which was included in this year's budget. Its direct effect will be to increase by that specific amount the price of consumer goods. By adding another $72 million a year to the cost of manufactured goods to be exported, in competition with other countries in the international market, we shall again be adding to the problem of inflation.
We of the opposition cannot accept this increase of 30 per cent in premiums without additional benefits to the employees. It is true that 80,000 more contributors will be added to the fund. By adding 80,000 more contributors and by choosing those contributors, as I said earlier, from a class which earns from $5,000 to $6,000 a year, the government is doing nothing else but setting up a pretext to get out of the dilemma in which it finds itself.
What about adding to those who should receive benefits from the unemployment insurance fund those that the government promised during the last campaign would be added? What about adding the workers employed on Canadian farms? What about those eastern Canadian farmers who have to employ lumbermen to cut pulpwood on their privately owned wood lots. In my constituency of Gloucester and in other sections of the maritime provinces farmers have substantially large wood lot holdings and they depend on the sale of pulpwood and lumber for their cash revenue. They cannot get any

help to cut this wood because they cannot guarantee unemployment insurance benefits?
We have heard at different times that one of the reasons why the unemployment insurance fund was being depleted is that fishermen have been made eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. The total amount paid to the fishermen during the winter of 1958 or 1959 is much less than the $10 million which was lost by the sale of bonds in 1958. This, notwithstanding what the Minister of Finance tried to explain a few minutes ago, is nothing else but pure robbery of the workers' savings in the unemployment insurance fund. Any insurance company which operated on such a basis would certainly not be in business very long.
Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) addressed a question to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). He suggested that on several occasions a minister of labour had asked the advisory committee to produce reports and make summaries in respect of amendments to the act and that these were not tabled because they were not required to be under the statute. But the Prime Minister did not draw any difference between the reports made in 1955 and the one referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the Leader of the Opposition.
It is true that the previous minister of labour asked the advisory board on certain occasions to produce certain reports and make summaries in respect of amendments to the act and that these were not tabled because they were not required to be under the statute. But the previous minister of labour did not hide from members of the house the fact that amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act were submitted to the unemployment insurance advisory committee for its approval as provided under the act. On January 11, 1955, when speaking on amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, Mr. Gregg, the then minister of labour, said, as found on page 80 of Hansard:
There is just one other point I wish to mention. It is something which I forgot to include in my first remarks. This bill has been submitted to the unemployment insurance advisory committee which is provided for under the act, and has been approved by them. Very shortly, of course, the larger bill will also be submitted to them.
The then minister of labour advised the house that the advisory committee had been consulted with respect to the amendments. Again, on April 4, 1955, Mr. Gregg, speaking on amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, said, as found on page 2663 of Hansard:
When the unemployment insurance advisory committee met on December 14 last to review the
66968-9-232
Unemployment Insurance Act amendments regarding seasonal benefits, it was of course necessary for the committee to have before it the views regarding this general revision as they were then held. Later when plans had further crystallized to the point where they were nearly the same as the amendments now proposed, a further meeting of the advisory committee was held on February 15. In order to review these final recommendations, as reflected in the actual bill, the committee has called a further meeting for tomorrow, April 5.
This is further evidence, Mr. Speaker, that the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission was consulted and the house was advised accordingly without the minister having to be requested to do so by the members of the opposition. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance should be reminded that under the previous Liberal administration the unemployment insurance fund was never in the precarious position it is today because, I repeat, of the mismanagement of the present government. This is why parliament is called upon to approve amendments which will place an extra burden on employers and employees without giving them any worth-while benefit in return. I might also add that when amendments were made to the Unemployment Insurance Act by the previous administration provision was made to obtain from the consolidated revenue fund the additional amount required to meet the needs of such amendments. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it will be impossible for the opposition to vote in favour of second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the impression in the country is that in order to replenish a fast depleting government account we must pass these amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. When I think that this actually amounts to an increase in taxes, when I think of the increases in taxes in the budget, I cannot help but think of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in Brantford on February 17, 1958, that "the humblest of our people will not be forgotten." I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is helping him to keep that promise.
The other day the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said that the purpose of the increase in rates was to bring the unemployment insurance account into better balance, but these particular facts strike me. First, there is no actuarial accounting to indicate to us whether the minister is raising rates too much or is not raising them enough to bring the account into much better balance. Second, there is a further great obligation or tax on employers and workers equal to one-third of the total tax increase imposed in the budget. This all occurs at a time when the Prime

Unemployment Insurance Act Minister himself said not long ago in Montreal that Canada was emerging from the recession more rapidly than any other country of the western free world. It also occurs at a time when the Minister of Finance has predicted a 7 per cent rise in the gross national product.
I should like to know why such conditions in the country would not bring about a building up rather than a depleting of the account. Under the former government the funds in the account certainly rose very rapidly under similar conditions.
I think the minister should be able to give us an estimate of the percentage increase in payments to take care of the extension of benefits from 36 to 52 weeks. We could then see how much of what will be raised will be needed to pay for the other increases in benefits which, after all, are very little. I think most of the increase is meant to look after seasonal unemployment. I met an executive of the pulp and paper industry the other day and he told me it was his opinion that it would cost that industry an extra $li million to $2 million in order to make the additional payments into the unemployment insurance fund. The workers in the industry will also have to pay a similar amount and will have it lifted from their pay envelopes.
The former government put money into the unemployment insurance fund from consolidated revenue to take care of seasonal unemployment and I think this government should do likewise. The workers who will have to contribute this money also have to pay more taxes because of the tax increases in the budget. They have to pay more sales tax. They have to pay increased cigarette and old pension taxes.
Now they are asked to assume all the taxes under these amendments in order to pay for seasonal unemployment. In spite of the promises made by the Prime Minister there has been no elimination of the waiting period. Today, I think for the first time, I heard a minister of the crown say that the government should be congratulated because of a $10 million loss in connection with a government account.
When the Prime Minister was in Welland he said that the government did not want relief and that is why they launched the winter works program. Certainly, I think there has been more relief paid, in my district at least, than there has been for a good many years. Unemployment insurance benefits certainly were not received by all the people.
I think, myself, that there has been a great


depletion in that account, and yet the municipalities have had to assume a great deal of the responsibility for people who were out of work.
While listening to the Minister of Finance a few minutes ago, two or three questions occurred to me. I heard him refer to the fact that there were $490 million in government securities in the fund-I may be mistaken, but I thought he said at face value or at current face value. I should like to add a few words to the remarks already made on this bill. The principle of unemployment insurance is, of course, sound and humane. It has made a substantial contribution to the freedom from want which was one of the principal clauses in the Atlantic Charter, the code on which the post-war policy of the free world was in fact based. During the past two years of recession the unemployment insurance fund was one of the main fenders between many people and penury. The establishment of this fund reflects the farsighted wisdom of the Liberal government which introduced it, and the forward looking statesmanlike approach which that government had.

However, it seems to me that the present bill will create an imbalance. While it is obviously desirable to stabilize the fund, it seems to me that the cost more than offsets the benefits. The increased benefits include a longer receiving period, increased from 36 weeks to 52 weeks. The wage level is raised, but the cost in premiums is also raised, yet the unit amount of the benefits remains the same.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, there are two kinds of unemployment. There is the unemployment which in normal times results when workers are temporarily out of work, but who normally would after a while be re-employed. Then there is the wholesale unemployment caused by the complete disappearance of jobs during an economic recession, such as that which has been historically associated with Tory times, and which has vexed the country for nearly two years. The former can be insured against, but the latter should be dealt with by an outright government grant. It is because of the fact the bill does not provide for outright government assistance, so that the cost can be borne by all, that I shall oppose this bill.

Mr. Chairman, at the time of adjournment of this debate last Friday night I was pointing out that our economic recovery depends to a very large degree on the employment of human resources, and that inflation and unemployment were the twins of misery besetting our communities today. The government is no doubt aware of the consequences of the evils of unemployment, but what are they doing about it? They certainly are not doing what they did when in opposition; that is plain when one reads their speeches in Hansard of 1955, 1956 and 1957, I do not wish to belabour the point by reading excerpts from these speeches at this time because I realize that my friend the minister, who has had a rough time during the past couple of days, is anxious to have the estimates approved without delay to enable him to proceed to the Geneva labour conference. May I extend to him sincere best wishes for an enjoyable time and safe journey.
However, I have here an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of January 24, 1959 which has a bearing on the situation and which I wish to read. It is as follows:
Mr. L. B. Pearson's colleagues in the House of Commons have been at some pains to reply to the personal attack made on their leader by Prime Minister Diefenbaker. The Prime Minister had lectured Mr. Pearson on his statistical references to unemployment and to the economic situation generally, saying that such remarks were "not in keeping with his responsibilities as Leader of the Opposition at a time when world conditions are difficult and trying, when the communist world
Supply-Labour
attacks the free world economically as never before." Mr. Pearson, in a word, was rocking the boat.
On that occasion Mr. Diefenbaker had scoffed at Liberal warnings about the state of the economy. Last year, he said, Canadians "worked more, earned more, spent more and saved more" than ever before. A few days later Mr. Paul Martin had an opportunity to comment on this statement, finding on the basis of official figures that Canadians had actually worked less, earned less and spent less, in terms of real dollars, than in the last year the Liberals were in office.
As for the charges that the opposition leader was talking in such a way as to instil fear into the Canadian people, Mr. Lionel Chevrier pointed out that some highly responsible men had expressed quite similar views. One of these was Cardinal Leger, who in a recent pastoral letter said that the unemployment situation "requires the intervention of government to take new and audacious steps." And Mr. Martin listed half a dozen heads of Canadian banks who had all spoken in the gravest terms of the problem of inflation.
In his own days in opposition, as Mr. Chevrier reminded the house, Mr. Diefenbaker had been less cheery about preaching "doom and gloom". In March, 1955, when there had been a fairly sharp, though temporary, upsurge of unemployment, he had accused former Prime Minister St. Laurent of remaining silent "in the face of a problem that wrings the hearts of the people". But if the Prime Minister feels that the people ought to be spoken to soothingly so as not to get them all upset, he does not always set a good example in that respect. When meeting a delegation from the Canadian Labour Congress, for example, he told it that the Russians are staging a "terrifying" trade offensive aimed at undermining the economies of western countries.
This is more apt to give a listener the chills than anything uttered by the leader of the opposition.
Just a few moments ago the Minister of Labour made reference to the present employment situation and claimed that it was much better than it was. I am very pleased and happy to hear about that, but unfortunately his statement does not apply to the city of Fort William. Here I have the figures with respect to unemployment in Fort William. I am quoting from the weekly statistics compiled by the unemployment insurance office of the city of Fort William. On December 5, 1957, there were 2,075 people seeking employment; on December 4, 1958, there were 2,522; on January 2, 1958 there were 2,975 people seeking employment, and on January 21, 1959 there were 3,343; on February 6, 1958 there were 3,297 people seeking employment, and on February 5, 1959 there were 3,836; on March 6, 1958, there were 3,639 people seeking employment, and on March 5, 1959, 3,822; on April 3, 1958 there were 3,727 people seeking employment and on April 2, 1959 there were 3,882; on May 7, 1959 there were 2,619 people seeking employment.
All these figures indicate that so far as the city of Fort William is concerned the employment situation is no better than it

Supply-Labour
was. In fact it keeps getting worse, unfortunately. It is obvious the statistics are not likely to inspire any degree of confidence in the present state of our economy. Therefore, it is imperative that something should be done immediately to lay the foundation for the cure of unemployment.
One of the puzzling paradoxes of our time lies in the fact that while the personal incomes of Canadian workers in 1958 reached the highest figure in their history, averaging an annual income of $3,534, and while farmers, too, enjoyed their biggest earnings on record, with $2.8 billion, an average of 405,000 Canadians were out of work in 1958, while all those billions of dollars were being made and spent. The average still holds at that rate today. Some 24,000 fewer Canadians were employed last year than were employed the year before-5,722,000 against 5,746,000.
The appointment of an advisory board with representatives from labour, industry, agriculture and the universities to help in dealing with the long term problems of production and employment, as advocated by the Liberal party under the leadership of the hon. member for Algoma East, should be considered by this government without delay. A much needed service to the nation would be rendered if action were taken to implement this proposal. I submit that the problem of unemployment transcends any other with which the government is faced. We of the opposition would be delighted to co-operate with the government in any measure designed to bring about a solution to the cancer-like curse of unemployment.
One cannot speak of labour without giving some consideration to that army of workers known as the civil service. These men and women, working silently and efficiently, dedicated for the most part to the service of their country, very much like an army disciplined by an archaic code which deprives them in many instances of a voice to vent their feelings or opinions because of fear that their jobs may be placed in jeopardy, should be granted a new charter. I suggest the Minister of Labour should recommend to his cabinet colleagues that the time has come to place all workers of the civil service below the executive rank on the same footing as workers who are employed in industry, and that they be given the same bargaining rights as any other group.
There should also be a study made to determine whether or not there are infringements on labour rights to organize in Canada. I believe that a clear-cut policy by the government on the rights of labour and

management should be made plain for all to understand, in order to avoid unnecessary labour disputes.
I have received letters from my own constituency reflecting dissatisfaction within the staff of the Post Office Department. The information I have is that their shift work is placed on a seven-day week. One letter disclosed that grievances which were taken up with the district director of postal services were not taken care of and that in consequence, the morale of the employees has suffered considerably.
Perhaps the minister would use his good offices in order to have an investigation made of the situation in the post office in Fort William.

Mr. Chairman, at the hour of adjournment I was indicating that the labour relations in the Fort William post office are not what they should be. I, therefore, would ask the minister to have an investigation made and if there is something wrong at that point I am sure there must be other places with similar complaints. It must be borne in mind here that the average civil servant will not complain for fear of discrimination.
I appeal to the minister to consider giving all our civil service employees a new charter in which there should be an outline of the rights of an individual to join any organization or political party of his choice. While this government claims that it does not favour patronage, it has been guilty of causing honest working men to be fired from their jobs because of political leanings or affiliations.
The charge has been made on more than one occasion that the Liberal government when in power were far more patronageconscious than the present government. Be that as it may, I for one would not make a single excuse for any government using their power to fire a person because of political affiliations. I look upon such an act as one of the most despicable outrages that anyone could commit, regardless of political stripe.
There is one particular question which I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour and that is the premises occupied at the present time by the unemployment insurance commission at 123 north May street in Fort William. It is the former post office building, erected in 1904. The unemployment insurance commission has been

occupying the premises since August, 1946. Since that time the steady growth and development of Fort William and the surrounding area find the premises occupied at the present time totally inadequate as to space, and unsuited structurally for handling the heavy volume of traffic peculiar to the unemployment insurance commission. The foreseeable space required for the next 10 years by the unemployment insurance commission office is 14 to 16 thousand square feet. The present 5,800 square feet reveal the lack of adequate working facilities, the congested conditions, which clearly indicate the present need for new premises as soon as possible.
The site occupied at the present time by the armouries, a federal government building, at 323 north Archibald street, would provide ample space for a new building to house the unemployment insurance commission office staff. The armouries building has been condemned and is to be torn down. Crown Assets Corporation has advertised for offers for the demolition and removal of the building from the site. The property belongs to the federal government and all that remains to be done is for the Department of Public Works to inspect the site and the unemployment insurance commission to approve the plans. This project should not present any difficulty to the government, financially or otherwise. I express the sincere hope that the minister will look upon the project with favour, as the present accommodation and facilities are totally inadequate. All one has to do to be convinced of the necessity of a new building is to go by on north May street, next to the premises of the Fort William Times Journal, to see long double queues of unemployed people lined up on the sidewalk waiting for something to come. Perhaps the minister may indicate that a new building is under consideration.
Finally, I submit that the greatest problem facing this government is the problem of checking rising costs and prices by creating more jobs and by producing more.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose it is true that we live in a country where winter unemployment has been traditional. I come from a province where there is probably on the average more winter unemployment than is experienced in any of the other nine provinces of Canada. I suppose generally we give the excuse that winter unemployment is a matter of winter weather; but perhaps over the last four or five years we have come to realize that winter unemployment is not altogether a matter of winter weather in
Supply-Labour
Canada. It may now be a matter of our thinking and it also may be a matter of habit.
In my own province of Newfoundland winter unemployment is a situation that we have had for many, many years. It is true it is largely due to winter weather but it is also largely due to the type of economy which we have, a type of economy which has been partly accepted by us and partly imposed on us. I suppose another reason why we do have more winter unemployment across Canada is the fact that many of our primary industries are outdoor industries.
But I believe that the time is at hand when winter unemployment will be reduced a good deal. Our secondary industries will catch up with the outdoor primary industries and there will also be a change in our thinking due to the fact that more people are becoming concerned as to the ill effects of unemployment during the winter months. I believe that the winter unemployment we have in this country can be reduced a great deal by concerted attack on the problem not only by the federal government but by provincial governments, municipal governments, employers, all those who are directly and indirectly concerned and all those who feel that for every man day that is lost in Canada some part of the country must suffer.
We have examples of how winter unemployment can be reduced. Take the construction industry which normally composes between 7 and 10 per cent of all industry in Canada. Yet its contribution to winter unemployment in years gone by has been much greater than those figures. Nonetheless over the last two or three years we have begun to see that by the use of different methods winter unemployment even in this segment of our economy can be reduced. Today jobs are being carried on in the winter time. Concrete is poured in zero weather and construction is carried on under cover with the result that the construction industry today is not hampered by winter weather as it used to be years ago. A very good example is the paint industry. In years gone by the paint and painting industry did most of its work in the spring and summer with very little during the winter months. But lately we have seen a larger percentage of employment in this industry during the winter months. Various methods have been introduced by which winter unemployment can be reduced.
But I say again that it is not altogether a matter for the federal government. It is a matter for the provincial governments also and everybody else interested in seeing

Supply-Labour
that every man in this country is employed for as long as it is possible for him to be employed. All phases of the economy must co-operate if we are to reduce winter unemployment to the level to which I believe it can be reduced.
During the past winter and in other years gone by the unemployment insurance commission endeavoured to set up committees all across the country to devise methods to decrease winter unemployment. In my own area a committee was set up under the manager of the unemployment insurance commission and I know that a great deal of effective work has been done. At this time I should like to extend to him, the members of his committee and the staff hearty congratulations for the work they have done under most difficult circumstances. I believe that with the encouragement of the federal Department of Labour they can continue their work and produce better results in the years that lie ahead.
In the field of labour the past year has been a most difficult one for my brother Newfoundlanders. The fishery has brought in far less returns to the fishermen than is the case in an average year. There is far less employment in the pulp and paper industry with the result that many men living along the coast of Newfoundland have not had the employment possibilities that have been open to them in years gone by. We have not been able to take advantage of the winter works program in the same way that many other provinces have for the simple reason that we do not have the same municipal set-up that is found in the other nine provinces of Canada. The 50-50 deal, for example, imposes some hardship on municipalities that even in the summer months have not sufficient money to be able to do the work that needs to be done. Under the regulations of the present winter employment program our municipalities are far less able to take advantage of the offer of the federal government.
The Department of Labour, of course, has agreements not only with municipalities but also with unorganized areas through the provincial governments. There are many places in Newfoundland where I think it would be very difficult to organize any winter works program and I suggest to the Minister of Labour that possibly it would be much more effective to endeavour to get what works can be started under way as early in the spring as possible. That is not only true in the case of federal works but all other types of works that are carried on.
Last year when we were considering suggestions for a winter works program I thought that one winter works program

which could have been undertaken on the west coast of Newfoundland was the improvement of Canadian National telegraphs service in that section of the province. If improvements had been decided upon a good deal of winter employment could have been given to loggers who would have been able to cut the necessary poles and at this time of the year considerable employment could have been given by Canadian National telegraphs in constructing a line down the west coast of Newfoundland in an area where communications are worse now than they have been at any time in the last 30 years. There was a time when communications existed all down that coast but over the years of the depression and the years of commission government the service was allowed to drop. It is necessary now to restore it and I believe that a winter works program could well be provided in this area by agreement between the Minister of Labour and Canadian National telegraphs to cut the necessary poles during the winter months and then later in the year have the line rebuilt along that section of the coast.
I say again that in those places where it is not possible to carry on a regular program of winter works it might be a very good thing indeed if those works that are to be started could be commenced very early in the year. I am going to give two examples. I cannot say that I am giving them merely as examples and am not complaining because in actual fact I am complaining to a certain extent. Last year public works began to build a harbour at Codroy on the west coast of Newfoundland and during the latter months of the year a good deal of work was done. When winter came the work was stopped. Even though we have had pretty fair weather in that section of Newfoundland for the last four weeks there has been no sign to date that the work will be resumed on this project. I believe this is a fairly good example of what could be done if work that is to be carried on during the year could be started as early as possible.
I give another example and while I am using it as an illustration I am also complaining. The Minister of Fisheries, who has been very kind in his efforts to attack our problems in Newfoundland and has always given a sympathetic hearing to our suggestions was able to have a portable bait depot sent to Norris Point in Bonne bay last year. The bait depot has been there since last fall. The fishermen are now ready to take up the lobster fishery after a long hard winter when they had very little income. Yet, they are not able to take advantage of the lobster fishery at this particular time because

they are still hampered by a lack of bait. While this particular bait depot has been there for nearly six months now, it is still not in operation. I hope that it will be very shortly.
I say again that this has been a very difficult winter in Newfoundland. Although the latest figures on unemployment are beginning to go down, and 1 am grateful to be able to say that, in my area at the moment there are 6,132 unemployed, and that is a reduction of about 600 from a week earlier. Nevertheless, we do have a large percentage of the population of Newfoundland on relief. During the whole of the month of March the number of heads of families unemployed amounted to 7,018, representing a total of 37,321 persons. When one realizes that the population of Newfoundland is 420,000, one recognizes that 37,000 is a large percentage of that population to be on relief. Of this number who are on relief, 6,078 are employable, that is the number of employable heads of families, representing 34,359 people.
During the debates on unemployment and employment that we have had in the last months one or two references have been made to election promises made by members of this government as they went across the country during the campaigns of 1957 and 1958. When the Prime Minister was at Brantford on February 7, 1958, he said this:
The humblest of our people will not be forgotten. The people who are unemployed will not be in the false position of being put on relief.
Yet here, even in the middle of the fifth month of the year, we still have almost 10 per cent of the people of Newfoundland on relief.
May I pass on now, Mr. Chairman, to one or two other points which I should like to make. I should like to mention very briefly vocational training and training for the unemployed. I believe that these two services provided by the federal government, by agreement with the provincial governments, are at this time particularly important. We have seen in the newspapers during the last few weeks numerous references to the relationship which exists between the level of education and the rate of unemployment. This is a task not only for the federal government, but for the provincial governments, for education officials and for all employees.
I suggest we do live in an age of automation, an age when greater demands are being made for trained personnel. I suppose it is true, too, that automation does produce temporarily a certain percentage of unemployment. But I think in the long run it does produce more jobs for those who are qualified to take them.
Supply-Labour
I would suggest, therefore, not only to this government but also to the officials in my own province, that more attention be paid to the program of vocational training and to training of the unemployed.
We live here in Canada in a country which has many natural resources, and the greatest will be its people, particularly the young people. The population in Canada has one-third of its total composed of people less than 20 years of age. All these young people can make a great contribution to the future of Canada if they are properly trained to take part in those things which they are equipped to do.
I was glad to hear the minister refer to the older worker. I believe that here we have a very serious problem facing this country, when a man or woman at the age of 40 can be debarred from certain classes of work and referred to as an older worker. I was pleased to hear the minister say he was going to give some attention to this problem. I would suggest to him he not only give attention to the older worker of 40 years of age, but also to the older worker in his sixties. We are living in a land where the span of life has been lengthened. 1 am sure that many people who are considered older workers at 40 years of age or who are discharged from their jobs at 65 years of age still have contributions to make in some fields.
May I refer to unemployment insurance again? I bring up a pet problem of mine. It is not one that involves a large number of people, but I think it is grossly unjust. During the past winter of 1958-59 and also the winter of 1957-58 I did have a number of young men in my constituency who were not able to find work in the fishing industry or the lumbering industry. They were living in small settlements where there was absolutely nothing to do, so they decided that for two or three of the winter months they would go back to school and attempt to improve their standing in English, arithmetic and perhaps history and geography. They were not taking the whole course that was given at the local school, but just taking those subjects that would be of help to them. I thought it was a very commendable thing for young men past school age to do. There was nothing else left for them to do, except sit at home and draw their unemployment insurance. If they went back to school to improve their educational standing, I thought it would be a sound thing to do. However, the moment they entered the school door their unemployment insurance benefits were cut off. I believe that this is eminently unfair, and I would present this problem to the Minister of Labour, not as a problem which involves a large number of people but as one

Supply-Labour
that is very serious from the standpoint of justice. I hope that on some future occasion he will be able to give some attention to a problem which, after all, is serious for those people concerned.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would hope that during the coming months, and before too long, the Minister of Labour will be making plans for his unemployment program for the coming winter. I hope that the plans will be made far ahead of time and they will be as effective as possible in reducing the number of men who are unemployed in the wintertime, many of whom have been unemployed for a large part of the year.

Mr. Chairman, as it was not possible under the rules of this house as interpreted by the Speaker yesterday and today to deal with one of the matters relating to the debate which preceded this one, at this particular moment when we are dealing with the estimates of the Department of Labour we are forced, indeed we have a duty to refer to a matter which we on this side of the house regard as a one of importance. I refer to the failure of the government and the Minister of Labour to table in this house a report of the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission relating to the unemployment insurance fund.
In his speech today the minister sought to indicate that what he had done was no different from what had been done on four other occasions by his immediate predecessor. He referred us to a number of reports of the advisory committee which were tabled by him during the course of his speech. I had an opportunity of looking over these four reports of the unemployment insurance advisory committee during the dinner recess. From examining these four reports I think it is clear that these were reports of the committee that do not cover matters that come under sections 89 and 90 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. These were reports that had nothing whatsoever to do with the fund, certainly with the fund in the context of sections 89 and 90. Any hon. member who wishes to take the trouble to peruse these reports will find confirmation of what I have said.
The situation is briefly this. A report was made by the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission on August 18, 1958. That report was tabled in this house. That report dealt with matters having to do with the fund and the perilous position in which that fund seemed to be, in the judgment of the advisory committee. In so far as this particular report is concerned, the act was fully complied with. Section 89 is explicit on this point and it

bears repetition in this particular in this new debate. Section 89, subsection (1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act reads as follows:
89. (1) Within four months after the end of each fiscal year the advisory committee shall make a report to the governor in council on the financial condition of the fund as of the end of that fiscal year and shall also make a report to the governor in council on the financial condition of the fund whenever the advisory committee considers that the fund is or is likely to become, and is likely to continue to be, insufficient to discharge its liabilities, and may make a report on the financial condition of the fund at such other times as the advisory committee may think fit.
As I say, this report was tabled in accordance with the act. The other day I asked the Minister of Labour if there was another report of the advisory committee. I gave notice of my intention to ask that question and on the orders of the day the minister indicated that he had not had time to prepare the reply to my question of which, as I say, notice had been given. I readily understand that the minister who is a busy man could justifiably and readily offer that reason for not having a reply ready at the time. After all, the minister is a man with great preoccupations and responsibilities. But later in the day, after I pressed him again or interrogated him again during the course of his speech during that afternoon, when he was explaining the principles of the amendments which he proposed to the Unemployment Insurance Act, he indicated that there had been a second report. He explained, however, that it was a report of a different category from the one to which I have just made reference; that it was a report that he himself had initiated; that he had asked the advisory committee to look into certain matters previously covered in their report of August 18. That report, however, he insisted was not a report of the same kind as the report which required tabling. During the course of the debate we endeavoured to pursue this matter but, as I said, under the interpretation of the rules by the Speaker we were precluded from so doing. It is now our duty to proceed further in connection with this matter.
There can be no doubt about the statutory obligation. I call the attention of the committee to section 90, subsection (2) which reads as follows;
(2) The minister shall lay every report made under section 89 before parliament within thirty days after it was submitted to the governor in council, or if parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first thirty days thereafter that parliament is sitting.

If the minister assigned a particular responsibility to the advisory committee, I am not going to quarrel with that except to say that the report is not the kind of report envisaged by these sections, and if it reports on the fund it must be addressed to the governor in council. Consequently under the statute that I have just referred to it must be tabled in this house.
Hon. members who are new to this house may wonder why we in the opposition place such emphasis on this matter. We do so for two reasons. First, because it is our duty to point out if, in our judgment, an act has not been fully complied with by the government. Not that we charge the minister with any criminal act, as was suggested the other night; that is not the intention. Everyone knows that the Minister of Labour did not for any sinister purpose fail to comply with the act. That is not the point. But if under our system of government we are to adhere to its principles, we must as the opposition take every opportunity to see that the law is fully observed.
That was done in this house in 1949, and those of us in this group and other members who were here at that time will well remember when we had a protracted debate in this house centered on an allegation made by the present Prime Minister, as well as by the present Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood, that the minister of justice of that time had not tabled a report pursuant to the obligations imposed on him under the Combines Investigation Act. They pointed out that the then minister of justice had failed to comply with the statute. We had endless days of debate and we had placed on Hansard words that undoubtedly have much to do with the inspiration which has persuaded the present Prime Minister to introduce in this house a bill of rights, which ultimately I understand is to come, a bill which has been so widely criticized because of its inadequacies and its failure to take into account the obligations of the provinces, and to recognize the constitutional difficulties involved in the bill of rights as a result. What does it mean? I will paraphrase the words of the Prime Minister. This means something that is fundamental to the preservation of this free parliament. These are the words of the Prime Minister.
Let us see what the Prime Minister had to say about this. Oh, it is all right for the Prime Minister to rise today and give us a lecture and tell us it was his duty to point out to us that we had no right to persist in debate. He acted as the custodian of the rights and privileges of this house, but he forgot to remind us that when he was sitting on this
Supply-Labour
side there was no one more persistent, day in and day out, in reminding us of our obligations as members of parliament to live up to the letter of the law. On the occasion I refer to he was criticizing the minister of justice because he had not tabled a report; because, seemingly, he had violated the act. No one was saying, as the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood, was fair enough to point out, that there was any dishonest intention on the part of the minister of justice any more than anyone is suggesting to the Minister of Labour that he had acted dishonestly. Anyone who knows the Minister of Labour knows that all we are doing is simply to point out that in our judgment the act has not been observed by him.
I think it would be useful to note, for the benefit of posterity and of those hon. members who have come to this parliament for the first time, these words of the Prime Minister, these memorable words, as the right hon. gentleman said referring to some words of mine in another context the other day.

Parliament has the right to expect that ministers of the crown shall live up to the provisions of statutes passed by parliament; for if these be not lived up to, parliamentary responsibility ends, and a contempt of parliament occurs which should not be permitted to pass uncensured.
The minister stated that the facts and conclusions in this report were, in his opinion, unjustified. That statement does not answer or justify the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) failing to discharge his obligatory responsibilities under the provisions of an act passed by parliament. Only three years ago in this house I was one of those who stated that in my opinion-and I know there were some who criticized me for this view-we should alter the provision with regard to publishing these reports in order that no one should be found guilty before the bar of public opinion without having the opportunity of answering in the courts.

And, as reported at page 2065 of Hansard of November 22, 1949 the hon. member for Greenwood, quoting from that authority, pointed out:
With us every official, from the prime minister down to a constable or a collector of taxes, is under the same responsibility for every act done without legal justification as any other citizen.

Here is what the hon. member for Greenwood said:
Let me remind hon. members that in respect of the ordinary citizen the law moves automatically, and it calls for him to account for what he has done. But, so far as I understand the constitution, the only bodies that can move against ministers when they break the law is, first of all, public opinion-and I shall come to that later-and, second, this House of Commons, which rejoices in the title of the High Court of Parliament.

Yet I suggest that in spite of all, in spite of the wise things that have been said here, the public of this country has not yet registered what has happened.
And the hon. member for Greenwood continued:
I said a moment ago it is hard to believe that men whom we like-
And that applies to the Minister of Labour
-and meet happily-
And that applies to the Minister of Labour
-and who have much good to their credit-
And that certainly applies to the Minister of Labour
-could do this wrong thing. And it may be that in some curious way they did not quite intend to do what was wrong.
I certainly believe that of the Minister of Labour. But what I am pointing out is that the failure to place this report on the table has deprived the public and parliament of the opportunity to be fully seized of the considered opinion of the advisory committee whose business it has been for some years to advise on these matters.
But the hon. member for Prince Albert, now Prime Minister, did not stop at one single speech. He came back to this matter, and I find that on November 22, 1949 he went on to complain once more about the failure of the minister of justice. He said, as reported at page 2091:
It was fairly obvious-and as I listened to him I sympathized with him-
He was referring to the minister of justice
*-that he realized what he had done was unjustifiable, inexcusable and a contravention of principles going back to the Bill of Rights, which declared among other things that no government or executive can suspend the law of the realm in any particular without parliament.
What the Prime Minister said that day certainly applies today.

I thank the committee. I will not take very long. I just want to complete those memorable words of the Prime Minister. He said at page 2092 of Hansard of November 22, 1949, in concluding his argument after a speech that lasted I suppose the usual time permitted under our rules:
That is no justification. Indeed, if anyone in this country had known during the 10 months' period that the minister had broken the law, as he did, His Majesty's courts could have been applied to in order to protect His Majesty's subjects, under a writ of mandamus, which would direct the minister to live up to the law. He concealed the report, and one explanation is this: we did not agree with the terms of the report. Is there anything in section 27 of the act that gives the government discretion to say they may break the law because they do not agree with the terms of a report; that they may break the law because after consideration, even honest consideration, they feel it should be broken? If that be an excuse for breaking the law, how many people in this country would feel like breaking the income tax law, or any other laws passed by parliament? Expediency, or the desire to prevent argument between high civil servants, afford no excuse in extenuation or otherwise for what has taken place in connection with this report.
I say to the minister, even assuming for purposes of argument that he was correct in saying that the four reports tabled today by him and addressed to his predecessor came under section 89 of the act, that would not justify or provide him with a satisfactory reply to the allegation and to the arguments that we have made in this context regarding this matter. However, I have indicated that these four reports do not refer to the state of the fund, and consequently do not come under section 89, or under section 90 (2). Therefore, I say to the Minister of Labour that if the advisory committee, when it is properly constituted once again, when the labour representatives are returned to their function, if they are going to be or if new ones are going to be appointed- the committee is not now legally in existence under section 19 (1) of the act-do make a report with regard to the state of the fund in any way the minister, I know, will not hesitate to table that report so that parliament will have the benefit of the judgment of the members of the committee and so that we can make an assessment as to whether or not the recommendations of the committee are satisfactory.
How valuable it would be to have had the report tabled on August 18 last and to have known that the committee felt that because of the perilous condition in which the fund was it was thought that the contribution
Supply-Labour
of the federal government should be increased. That is in conformity with the stand that we have taken with regard to this measure, a measure which will go to a committee where we hope it will be possible to improve the bill and to remove some of the burden on the employers and on the employees which we feel has been imposed upon them unjustly.
The minister has tabled not only the four reports but the minutes of some of the meetings. He certainly tabled the minutes of the meetings of July 24 and 25, 1950. It would be of the greatest value certainly to us in this house and to the committee if we had the minutes of the meeting of August 18, so we could find out whether or not the advisory committee detailed the reasons for the statements it made when it observed that there should be an increase in the federal contribution so that there could be an adjustment and so that the contributions from each of the contributing parties would be made equal; in other words, that the contribution from the government would be made equal to one-half that of the combined contributions from employers and employees.
I simply have this further observation to make, Mr. Chairman. The way to preserve the rights of parliament is not by a bill that does not take into account the constitutional responsibilities of other levels of government in Canada. It does not consist in general statements declaratory of one's belief in the freedom of the subject. The way to guarantee civil liberties and the rights of parliament-and these words I address particularly to the Prime Minister-is by seeing to it that the law of the land is observed by everyone.
