speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the main reason why I want to make remarks on this particular estimate has to do with something that has been debated very much in the last while, namely the unemployment insurance commission. The aspect that I wanted to touch on is one which I do not think anyone has been after as yet. In effect, it is a request to the minister or to the department to consider the possibility of getting some outside agency-perhaps one of the groups that is making efficiency studies-to come in and look at the unemployment insurance commission operation, to see how the operation would stand up to the general accusation that I think every member of parliament hears, namely that there is a great deal of abuse of this particular welfare arrangement.
I should like to make it very clear that I do not believe there are very many abuses, but these are the stories that are tending

Supply-Labour
to be exaggerated at all times. I do believe that when you get a situation where there is largely false propaganda being made about the operation of a fund such as this, the thing to do is to scotch it wherever possible. I notice that from representatives of management I get representations that the unemployment insurance idea is fine but there are very many abuses in relation to it; there are all sorts of people taking advantage of the fund who should not take advantage of it and we must wipe out those abuses. I think every once in a while it is important that the commission and those people who guide and administer it should tackle this particular problem which to a degree is one of public relations. I think the time has come to do that.
I notice that in my constituency during the past winter up to 25 per cent of the labour force was registered for unemployment insurance benefits. In the neighbouring constituency of Fort William, which is linked to it, the rate was not quite as high but almost as high. At the same time in my constituency I heard so often from people who are unemployed that there were a great many abuses. All my contacts with the unemployment insurance commission officials and with labour representatives in the area indicate that there would be a denial of this; but there is in existence this popular conception, or misconception, and I think it is one of the responsibilities of the minister, if he feels the fund and the whole concept are as worth while as he expressed in ringing tones this afternoon, to do the job. It is largely his responsibility to see that this type of false propaganda is scotched, if it is false propaganda, as I believe it is.
One of the other brief remarks I wanted to make about this particular department has to do with the Canada labour relations board. I am probably one of the few members of parliament who has ever been at a hearing of that board in any capacity, and I was not impressed with what went on there. It seemed to me that the proceedings were perhaps rather more informal than I think should be the case with such a body. I happened to appear before the board with a group making a representation which was turned down. The reasons for it being turned down were probably quite valid. I have no quarrel with them. But the mood or atmosphere of the hearing was something that I think would be considered by many people to be regrettable. When you have the kind of hearing where first names are being tossed back and forth between the members of the board who are judging the matter and people who are there with an interest in the case 
one cannot help but have the feeling that the person who is not on a first-name basis is on the outside and in a difficult position.
This is a minor complaint. I only saw one example of the workings of the board but as the minister has a direct relationship with the board I feel it is something that he might take into consideration. I would not want to suggest that the proceedings should be made a great deal more formal so that they would be like a court of law with all its formalities but if my experience is typical I suggest that there could be room for some of the people who appear before the board to feel that they are pretty well on the outside if they do not happen to know the members of the board on a first-name basis.
One other point I wish to make in connection with the department has to do with the question of annuities. As I think all members know, I brought up in the house not too long ago the subject of increased recompense for members of parliament. Since then I have had a number of communications and this particular one brings up a point in connection with annuities that I think is fairly valid. The letter is from Mr. J. F. Brister of 2323 Inglewood avenue, West Vancouver, B.C. The first part of the letter is nothing more than a condemnation of members of parliament who would go after more pay when old age pensioners and people like that are having a difficult time. This is not the place to answer that but he does go on to deal with the falsity of the whole government annuities approach as a result of inflation. He says in his letter:
I am bringing this matter to your notice because this matter of Canadian government annuities is one which simply screams for some sort of justice to be done on behalf of those who have been so hard hit due to having placed their faith in these government annuities and tried to provide for their own welfare in their old age.-
Regarding government annuities, the attached outlines some of the incentives and assurances which were embodied in an official brochure entitled "Canadian Government Annuities-Backed by the Whole Resources of the Dominion." From cover to cover this brochure extolled the great advantages and the security which would accrue to those who placed their trust in these annuities.
I suggest to you that it is the solemn duty of any government to honour the obligations which are clearly outlined in this official brochure and that justice in the most elementary sense demands that at least some of the enormous increase in government income should long ago have been channelled back to those unfortunates who placed their good dollars and their trust in these annuities.
The next paragraph may interest the minister.
I wish to make it clear that the responsibility for the plight of government annuitants today lies squarely on the shoulders of the late Liberal government who permitted inflation to creep upon

them while as a government no action was taken to arrest or offset the dangers which were gaining momentum with the passing of time but I repeat no action was taken. The onus to correct a grave injustice does fall upon all succeeding governments.
In conclusion and with regard to the present plight of government annuitants it will be noted as per attached that it is stated:
"In offering you now the benefits which Canadian government annuities provide, the government does so with one purpose in mind, that of making it possible for all within the borders of Canada to spend their old age in comfort and ease, a fitting and well-earned reward for an industrious life. This assures you a safe and profitable investment . . . with the certainty of a definite livable income when your working days are over."
The maximum permitted under the Annuities Act is $1,200 per annum.
Obviously there are difficulties in this particular regard. This gentleman is suggesting that people who put good dollars into annuities that have depreciated very much in value have in a sense been "suckered" by the overoptimistic advertising of the annuities scheme. It seems to me that the other point he is making is that the maximum of $1,200 for an annuity is nonsensical in the light of inflation and what has happened to the dollar. All I can suggest is that we should have a statement from the minister when we get to the annuities branch as to the views of the government on what has happened to these long time holders or builders-up of government annuities and, on the other hand, what is the government doing about acceding to the request of many people that the level of government annuities be raised above $1,200.
I know that the charge I have heard repeatedly is that the insurance company lobby is so powerful that the government is frightened to go ahead and raise the ceiling. I should like a yes or no or an explanation of that particular charge. I do not make it from my own knowledge. I am just repeating something I have seen in labour publications.
The final point I want to touch on is a personal one. It has to do with criticisms that have been made in the debate about one of the executive vice-presidents of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Stanley Knowles. He has been referred to by the young member for Hamilton South as a political hatchet-man and the hon. member for Winnipeg North had some very derogatory things to say about Mr. Knowles. It is not my position to state that Mr. Knowles is not open to attack. It is not my position to defend whatever he may be doing in his particular post, but I should like to remind the members who accuse him in such derogatory terms that for many years he was a member of this house, a member whose 66968-9-233
Supply-Labour
conduct and integrity were of such a standard that he was offered, we gather, the most senior and honourable post in this house. I should like to say to those who have made these vicious criticisms of this particular gentleman that his conduct throughout the time he was in the house, in terms of probity, integrity and fair dealing, should have been good enough to protect him from this worst kind of invective that he seems to gather in another post.

I should like to comment briefly on this item. First of all, I should

Supply-Labour
like to again express my regret that special arrangements were not made last fall to make unemployment insurance benefits available to all fishermen who suffered from the disastrous failure of the cod fishery in Newfoundland last year. I would ask the minister to keep in mind the possibility of making provision to look after such a contingency, if we are unfortunate enough to be faced with it again. The winter works program did not work out so well in Newfoundland. This was simply because the program was not applicable to Newfoundland.
However, there was one aspect of the winter works program which deserves commendation, and I refer to the construction of community stages. From an employment standpoint, this program was limited in its benefits, but from a utility standpoint the idea was sound and worth while. These community stages are needed, and with the loss of fishing property in southern Labrador and northern Newfoundland, the need is greater than it ever was before. A continuation of the program is very desirable. I would suggest to the minister that it is not too early to start to plan for another program to build community stages, the work to be done next fall and the following spring because work in the fall and spring is more important in the part of Newfoundland which I represent than work in the middle of the winter.
There is one type of industry which lends itself to winter work. I refer to the cutting of timber. I should like to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's. The cutting of telephone and telegraph poles for the C.N.T., the cutting of railway ties for the C.N.R. and the cutting of timber for wharves and breakwaters to be constructed by the Department of Public Works could be organized in a way that would give planned employment during the winter. The cutting of this timber could be organized in the vicinity in which the various projects are to be constructed.
There is another matter I should like to mention and that is the question of servicing the more remote areas in Newfoundland by unemployment insurance officials. This has been discussed before, and I was happy to hear a while ago that a program was being organized to supply fieldmen who would travel from outport to outport to assist people with their unemployment insurance problems. These officials could give advice and straighten out these problems at the source. I should like to say this is a fine, forward step, and I presume the program is being implemented as quickly as possible.

I should like to make a suggestion whereby I believe the service of existing unemployment insurance offices might be extended. The officials from the centres could, from time to time at set periods visit the nearby places. I have one place in mind which will serve as an illustration, and that is the seaport of Botwood, which is about 20 or 30 miles from Grand Falls. Grand Falls has a permanent unemployment insurance office. Last year the management of a union at Botwood requested that officials from the Grand Falls office spend a day or two in Botwood from time to time, timing their visits to coincide with payday, and thus assist people with their unemployment insurance problems. The union suggested that they would provide an office rent-free, light-free, and so on. Some plan of that nature, I think, would extend the services-

Thank you very much, sir; I shall be glad to do it.
There is one other point which has to do with employment rather than unemployment. There is a tendency in Newfoundland for those who are living near the large centres of population in which employment offices exist to get preference over those living in the remote areas when there are jobs available. This is only natural because they are on the spot. One way to offset this, I think, would be to keep the names of those who apply for jobs on file longer. I believe, as it stands now, after the names are on file for a while they are declared dormant and the newer applicants get consideration while the older ones are dropped. In view of the distances involved, and the fact that some people looking for work are living in the remote areas where communications are slow, I would suggest that a little special attention be given to these applicants from the distant places so they would get an equal chance.
Not long ago I was talking with an employment official, not connected with the government I hasten to add, who told me that the applicants from nearby were generally considered first because they were more readily available. They could be questioned as to their status, when they could commence work, their qualifications and so on. I imagine the same conditions would apply to employment officials of the Department of Labour. In conclusion, I would ask the minister to consider these few remarks and see that proper consideration is given to those who are handicapped as a result of living some distance away from the employment offices.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief remarks that I should like to make at this time. They are about a subject that has been touched on tonight but I think possibly a little bit more attention could be given to it. This matter was drawn clearly to my attention by an article I noticed in the paper today. It has to do with a situation that occurred in my own riding where three men had been convicted-in one case I believe there were 16 charges-of fraud in collecting unemployment insurance improperly. In fact, I believe they took time off from their work in order to collect their unemployment insurance cheques.
I think this is an extremely important matter. I do not know just how widespread this offence is across the country; but certainly if there were only these three cases, they are far too many. All this offence amounts to is nothing more or less than chiselling. Certainly even the people who a few years ago were extremely opposed to the idea of unemployment insurance and indeed to some other social benefits have come around now to the understanding that they are good and beneficial things for the working people of this country. But situations such as this one certainly give the opponents of unemployment insurance and other social benefits good ammunition with which to carry on their attacks on these social benefits.
There are two ways of dealing with this matter. One is a continuation and possibly an improvement, if possible, of the present method which is, of course, policing these things to the best of our ability. The other one, of course, is the one that is proposed by the opponents to this plan who say that, because this plan is being abused by a few people it should be abolished. We have seen that attitude in respect of this item and many other items of social welfare. It is said that people are going to abuse it, and that it should be abolished because people are just taking advantage of it.
I think we must look a little deeper into the matter in order to find the reasons for these abuses. I think a great deal of the difficulty is because of this theory that is so prevalent in our society, this something for

nothing idea. Certainly political parties are not free of guilt of proposing this idea. We are always going to give something for nothing and people are inclined to go along with this idea. Certainly our advertising across the country is to a great extent based on this false statement. We are always giving prizes for this and something else for that, and everybody is led to believe that he is getting something for nothing. There is no such thing in society, and I think the sooner we tell the people this, the better off we are all going to be. In fact, I sometimes think that this is the reason why the party I represent has not been more successful than it has been in this country. One of my colleagues in Timmins told me one time that the reason the C.C.F. has not been more successful is that we appeal to the unselfish side of people whereas the other parties appeal to the selfish side, and that is why they are so successful.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You are thinking of the selfrighteous side of people.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: However, I think that this is something that the minister should take into consideration. I think something could be done through the public relations branch of the department. I think a greater effort should be made to appeal to the basic honesty in people and to make them realize that in chiselling on the unemployment insurance fund and other benefits of that nature they are not only cheating the other people but are in fact jeopardizing the whole plan and defeating the very things that have taken many years to build up to the advantage of the Canadian working people.

Mr. Chairman, I have two questions on two different topics which I would like to put to the minister before this item carries. My first question deals with the community stage program or fishermen's stage program in Newfoundland. This program was put forward as part of a winter works program, and to that extent it involves the Department of Labour. But it is complicated in that it involves not only the Department of Labour and the Department of Fisheries, which makes some recommendation in this matter in connection with these projects, but also the Department of Public Works, which builds these stages.
Due to the fact that three departments are involved here, I do not want to miss an opportunity of getting some information about one aspect of this program which I should like to bring before the house, and it is this. There seem to be two kinds of programs in connection with the community stages, both going on at the same time. I know of two communities about ten miles

apart. In one community the stage is being built and the people are being paid by the department for their labour in connection with the building of it. In the other community only a short distance away the same thing is happening but the fishermen have to donate their labour; they are not getting paid for their labour at all.
I do not know to what extent this involves the minister's department, but I think it is something which should be brought to his attention, because if we are going to have a program of community stages, even if it is a winter works program and credit is taken for it as a winter works program, we should have the same treatment for all fishermen. We should not have the position where some donate their labour and some get paid for their labour. I see that the Minister of Public Works is in his seat and he can be sure that when his estimates come before the house I will have some important questions to ask him too; but I would like the Minister of Labour to clarify now to what extent his department is involved in this program, and whether he is at all responsible for this position.
